specPoints.text: understand why a catalyst does not affect the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction

know the effect of changing either temperature or pressure on the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction: an increase (or decrease) in temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction of the endothermic (or exothermic) reaction; an increase (or decrease) in pressure shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction that produces fewer (or more) moles of gas References to Le Chatelier's principle are not required

primer.text: From Reversible Reactions you already know that changes can run both ways at once. This note asks where the balance point sits, how temperature and pressure shove it, and why a catalyst cannot move it at all. Colour-change equilibria make the shifting balance visible to the eye.

lessons.title: Equilibrium position and temperature
lessons.opening: How much of each chemical survives at equilibrium depends on the conditions around the flask. This lesson introduces the principle chemists use to predict the shift and applies it to temperature changes.
keyPoints: The balance of reactants and products at equilibrium answers to the conditions.
A shift to the right means the forward reaction is favoured and more products form.
A shift to the left means the reverse reaction is favoured and more reactants form.
Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction of the endothermic reaction.
Lowering the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the direction of the exothermic reaction.

low.restatement: The balance point between the two directions is not fixed: heat it and the balance leans towards the heat-using direction, cool it and it leans towards the heat-releasing one. Leaning right means more products; leaning left means more reactants.
low.analogy: It is like a see-saw with people swapping sides when the rules change: the balance always tips towards whichever side the new rules favour.
low.examPointer: Name the direction of the shift and tie it to the endothermic or exothermic side.

medium.restatement: Changing the conditions moves the position of equilibrium, so temperature shifts favour one direction: hotter conditions favour the endothermic direction and cooler conditions the exothermic one. A right shift raises the amount of products and a left shift raises the amount of reactants.
medium.analogy: A thermostat in disguise: heat the room and the equilibrium does the opposite of what you did, absorbing the extra heat by running the cooling direction.
medium.examPointer: Answer temperature questions by first asking which direction absorbs the change, then name the shift.

check.stem: Heating an equilibrium mixture favours which direction?

options.text: The endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat
options.explanation: The system responds to heating by using up heat in the endothermic direction.

options.text: The exothermic direction, which releases more heat
options.explanation: Releasing heat would add to the disturbance, not oppose it.

options.text: Neither direction moves
options.explanation: Temperature shifts do move the balance.

options.text: Both directions equally
options.explanation: Equal shifts would change nothing, which is not observed.

check.stem: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. What does cooling the mixture do?

options.text: It favours the forward reaction, so more product forms
options.explanation: Cooling favours the heat-releasing side, which is the forward direction here.

options.text: It favours the backward reaction, so more reactant forms
options.explanation: The backward reaction is endothermic here and is favoured by heating.

options.text: The mixture changes colour to blue
options.explanation: Colour depends on the specific equilibrium, not on cooling alone.

options.text: The equilibrium is destroyed
options.explanation: The balance moves; it does not vanish.

check.stem: What does it mean for the position of equilibrium to shift right?

options.text: The forward reaction is favoured, so the amount of products increases
options.explanation: Right shifts enrich the product side of the equation.

options.text: The reactants increase in amount
options.explanation: That describes a left shift.

options.text: The reaction stops completely
options.explanation: Equilibrium mixtures never stop reacting.

options.text: The catalyst becomes more active
options.explanation: Catalysts do not take sides in the shift.

check.stem: Iodine monochloride and chlorine form iodine trichloride, with the forward reaction exothermic. On heating, the brown colour deepens. Why?

options.text: Heating favours the endothermic backward reaction, so more brown reactant forms
options.explanation: The shift runs left, enriching the dark brown starting materials.

options.text: Heating favours the forward reaction, so more yellow product forms
options.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic and is disfavoured by heating.

options.text: The product decomposes into oxygen
options.explanation: No oxygen is part of this equilibrium.

options.text: The thermometer itself darkens the liquid
options.explanation: The colour change is chemical, not instrumental.

check.stem: Which change would shift an equilibrium towards the exothermic direction?

options.text: Lowering the temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Cooling pulls the balance towards the heat-releasing side.

options.text: Raising the temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic side instead.

options.text: Adding a catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts never move the position.

options.text: Increasing the pressure of a gas equilibrium
options.explanation: Pressure shifts follow molecule counts, not heat.

lessons.title: Pressure and the molecule count
lessons.opening: Squeezing a gaseous equilibrium changes the balance too, but only gases feel the squeeze. This lesson counts molecules on each side of the equation and predicts the shift from the count alone.
keyPoints: Changes in pressure only affect gases in an equilibrium mixture.
Increasing the pressure favours the reaction producing the fewest gas molecules.
Decreasing the pressure favours the reaction producing the most gas molecules.
Equal numbers of gas molecules on both sides mean pressure has no effect on the position.
Pressure changes affect only the position of equilibrium, never the rates equally matched by a catalyst.

low.restatement: Push on a gaseous equilibrium and the balance slides towards whichever side packs fewer gas molecules. If both sides hold the same count, squeezing changes nothing about the balance.
low.analogy: It is like a crowded train: squeeze the carriage and people move to whichever end has fewer passengers standing.
low.examPointer: Count the gas molecules on each side before predicting any pressure shift.

medium.restatement: Raising the pressure of a gaseous equilibrium favours the direction that produces the fewest gas molecules, while lowering the pressure favours the direction producing more. When the gas counts match on both sides, pressure changes leave the position of equilibrium unchanged.
medium.analogy: A lift preferentially fills with the smallest group first; if both floors hold equal groups, squeezing the lobby sends no signal.
medium.examPointer: Write the molecule counts over each side, then quote the direction that the pressure change favours.

check.stem: Why does increased pressure favour fewer gas molecules?

options.text: Fewer molecules ease the crowding that the pressure increase created
options.explanation: The shift opposes the squeeze by reducing the gas count.

options.text: Fewer molecules are always faster
options.explanation: Speed is not the logic; the count is.

options.text: Because solids take up the extra pressure
options.explanation: Solids and liquids are unaffected by pressure changes here.

options.text: Because molecules shrink under pressure
options.explanation: Molecules do not shrink; the balance moves.

check.stem: In 2NO2 (g) turning into N2O4 (g), what does increased pressure do?

options.text: It favours the forward reaction, since two molecules become one
options.explanation: The product side holds fewer gas molecules, so pressure pushes the balance right.

options.text: It favours the backward reaction, since one molecule becomes two
options.explanation: Splitting into more molecules works against a squeeze.

options.text: Nothing, because both sides have equal counts
options.explanation: The counts are 2 and 1, not equal.

options.text: It turns the gas into a liquid
options.explanation: The equilibrium stays gaseous.

check.stem: A gaseous equilibrium has three molecules on the left and three on the right. What does increased pressure do?

options.text: Nothing to the position, because both sides hold the same gas count
options.explanation: Equal counts leave the balance unmoved by pressure.

options.text: It shifts the position to the left
options.explanation: No side has fewer molecules to favour.

options.text: It shifts the position to the right
options.explanation: The equal count blocks any shift.

options.text: It stops the forward reaction
options.explanation: Reactions continue at equilibrium regardless.

check.stem: Which observation would show a gaseous equilibrium shifting right after compression?

options.text: The colour deepens towards the product side of the equation
options.explanation: Enrichment of the product side shows itself as that side's colour strengthening.

options.text: The colour lightens towards the reactant side
options.explanation: That would indicate a left shift.

options.text: The gas turns into a solid
options.explanation: State changes are not part of the shift.

options.text: The readings become impossible to take
options.explanation: Compression leaves the mixture observable.

check.stem: Pressure changes do not affect the position when which condition holds?

options.text: The same number of moles of gas sits on each side of the equation
options.explanation: Matching gas counts leave the balance with nothing to prefer.

options.text: A catalyst is present in the mixture
options.explanation: Catalysts are irrelevant to pressure shifts.

options.text: The temperature is above room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature level does not cancel pressure effects.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic
options.explanation: Heat direction governs temperature shifts, not pressure ones.

lessons.title: Catalysts and dynamic equilibrium
sourceHeadings: The effect of catalysts on equilibrium
lessons.opening: A catalyst speeds reactions, so surely it should push the balance towards products. It does not, and the reason is elegant: it speeds both directions equally. This lesson proves that on the rate graph.
keyPoints: Catalysts leave the equilibrium position exactly where it was.
A catalyst increases the rate at which equilibrium is reached.
Forward and backward rates rise together, each sped up equally.
The concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium are the same with or without a catalyst.
On a rate graph the catalysed run flattens sooner but at the identical final level.

low.restatement: A catalyst helps both directions equally, so the balance point never moves; it is simply reached sooner. The final mixture is exactly the same, only faster in arriving.
low.analogy: It is like two escalators running at double speed in opposite directions: everyone moves faster, but the crowds on each floor end up the same.
low.examPointer: Say faster equilibrium, same position, whenever a question pairs catalysts with equilibrium.

medium.restatement: Because the catalyst lowers the barrier for both directions by the same amount, the forward and backward rates rise together and the position of equilibrium is unchanged. The equilibrium concentrations therefore match the uncatalysed case, with equilibrium simply arriving earlier.
medium.analogy: Two queues served by faster tills shorten at the same pace, so the split of shoppers between them never changes.
medium.examPointer: Explain the unchanged position through equal speeding of both directions, then read the flattening graph.

check.stem: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of equilibrium?

options.text: None: the position is unchanged
options.explanation: Catalysts speed arrival at equilibrium without moving it.

options.text: It shifts the position to the right
options.explanation: That would require favouring the forward direction, which catalysts never do.

options.text: It shifts the position to the left
options.explanation: No direction is favoured.

options.text: It depends on which catalyst is used
options.explanation: Every catalyst behaves the same way here.

check.stem: Why does a catalyst fail to move the equilibrium position?

options.text: It increases the rate of both the forward and backward reactions by the same amount
options.explanation: Equal speeding leaves the balance between the two untouched.

options.text: It is too small an amount to matter
options.explanation: Amount is irrelevant to the symmetry of the effect.

options.text: It stops both reactions completely
options.explanation: Catalysts speed reactions, never stop them.

options.text: It only helps the reverse reaction
options.explanation: Help is shared equally between directions.

check.stem: What does a catalyst change about an equilibrium system?

options.text: The time taken to reach equilibrium
options.explanation: Faster arrival is the one change a catalyst delivers.

options.text: The final amount of product at equilibrium
options.explanation: The equilibrium composition is identical either way.

options.text: The enthalpy change of the forward reaction
options.explanation: Energy differences between levels are untouched.

options.text: The colour of the final mixture
options.explanation: The same final composition has the same colour.

check.stem: On a graph of product amount against time, how does the catalysed run compare with the uncatalysed one?

options.text: It flattens sooner but reaches the identical final level
options.explanation: Faster approach with the same destination is the catalytic fingerprint.

options.text: It flattens later at a higher level
options.explanation: Neither the timing nor the level changes that way.

options.text: It never flattens
options.explanation: Equilibrium is still reached, only sooner.

options.text: It starts from a higher point
options.explanation: Both runs begin with no product.

check.stem: Why is the equilibrium composition the same with and without a catalyst?

options.text: The same balance between forward and backward rates is restored once equilibrium returns
options.explanation: Equilibrium composition depends on conditions, not on how quickly they are met.

options.text: Because catalysts remove the reverse reaction
options.explanation: Both directions continue at equilibrium.

options.text: Because catalysts change the temperature
options.explanation: Catalysts are not heat sources.

options.text: Because products destroy the catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts survive the reaction unchanged.

glossary.definition: The balance between reactants and products in a reversible reaction under given conditions.
A change that favours the forward reaction and increases the amount of products.
A change that favours the reverse reaction and increases the amount of reactants.
The state in which forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates with no net change.
The amount of a substance in a given volume, whose equilibrium value a catalyst cannot alter.
